newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi says committed to pensions reform.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi says committed to pensions reform.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi said in a magazine interview released on Thursday that he was committed to a serious reform of Italy's costly pensions system but against shifts in parliamentary alliances to obtain it.
Prodi also told the Panorama news weekly that reform of the welfare state could not "massacre pensioners".
"I want to tackle pensions reform seriously but I don't accept any improper swap between politics, parliamentary alliances and pensions," he told the magazine.

Opposition centre-right bloc leader Silvio Berlusconi has offered to work with the coalition on an early 1998 budget -- which the government says will send a strong signal of Italian stability ahead of European Economic and Monetary Union -- in return for a combined assault on welfare reform.
Prodi said penions reform must "make some order in overall social spending but not massacre pensioners".

Prodi is walking a political tightrope over pension cuts as he tries to stay within sight of European single currency goals while facing opposition to social spending reductions from a key parliamentary ally, the Communist Refoundation party.
European Commissioner Mario Monti said on Thursday that keeping the welfare state in Italy in its current form was "untenable" and warned that without change it was destined to fail.
According to European Union statistics, Italy spends less overall on its social services than the European average, but more on pensions.

Italy enacted some pension reforms in 1995 and agreed to review the situation in 1998, but a row has broken out over moves to bring the review forward to this year. Communist Refoundation and union leaders are opposed to an early review.
